questions.q: What is the narrator's primary internal conflict during the luncheon at Foyot's?
questions.a: The narrator's primary internal conflict is the clash between his extreme financial constraint (he has only eighty francs for the month and a modest lunch should cost fifteen francs) and his inability to refuse the woman's escalating demands because he is too young and flattered to say no. A wrong answer might focus only on the woman's greed or the narrator's hunger, missing the specific psychological tension of performative generosity versus private panic.

questions.q: Explain how the narrator's statement 'I was too young to have learned to say no to a woman' functions as both characterization and thematic foreshadowing.
questions.a: This statement characterizes the narrator as socially inexperienced, eager to please, and bound by gendered politeness norms of his time. It foreshadows the thematic arc: his youthful inability to set boundaries leads to financial ruin for the month, while the retrospective telling (twenty years later) shows he has since gained the wisdom to recognize the absurdity — and the woman's eventual weight gain becomes cosmic justice. A wrong answer would treat it as mere background information without linking it to the story's irony or the narrator's growth.

questions.q: Apply the 'Show, Don't Tell' principle: find two moments where Maugham reveals the narrator's panic through physical or behavioral details rather than direct statements of fear.
questions.a: 1) 'My heart sank a little' when caviar is requested — a physiological response showing dread of cost. 2) 'Panic seized me' while waiting for asparagus, followed by the concrete calculation of whether he has enough to pay the bill and his dramatic plan to pretend his money was stolen. A wrong answer might quote only direct statements like 'I was startled' without identifying the physical or behavioral manifestations of panic.

questions.q: Analyze how the first-person retrospective narrative (the older narrator looking back twenty years) changes the reader's perception of the protagonist compared to a purely present-tense narration.
questions.a: The retrospective voice adds layers of dramatic irony and self-awareness: the older narrator knows the outcome (he survived, she grew obese) and can comment with 'complacency' on the 'immortal gods' giving him revenge. This distance transforms the protagonist from a passive victim into a witty observer who crafts the anecdote for comic effect. A purely present-tense narration would heighten anxiety but lose the humorous framing and thematic closure. A wrong answer would claim the perspective doesn't matter or only mention 'we know his thoughts.'

questions.q: Evaluate whether the narrator's final remark — 'I'll eat nothing for dinner tonight' — is an act of resilience, sarcasm, or both. Justify with evidence from his internal monologue during the meal.
questions.a: It is both: resilience because he accepts the financial hit and plans to endure hunger (practical survival), and sarcasm because he delivers it as a witty retort to her hypocritical advice ('Follow my example... never eat more than one thing'), exposing her gluttony. His internal monologue ('I had the whole month before me and not a penny in my pocket') shows he is genuinely broke, making the joke a coping mechanism. A wrong answer would pick only one tone without acknowledging the duality that defines his humor.

questions.q: Create a 50-word diary entry the narrator might have written that night, capturing his voice, financial reality, and the irony of the woman's parting advice.
questions.a: Sample: 'June 12. Eighty francs gone. She ate salmon, caviar, asparagus, peaches, ice-cream, champagne — all while lecturing me on "one thing for luncheon." I smiled, paid, walked home empty-pocketed. Her parting shot: "Follow my example." Tonight I dine on air. Revenge is a dish best served twenty years later.' A poor entry would lack the ironic contrast between her words and actions, or omit the narrator's distinctive humorous resignation.
